name: Winged bean
summary: How Filipino farmers and backyard growers raise sigarilyas, the climbing bean with four winged pods. It is seeded direct beside poles or a fence and picked young for weeks once it starts bearing.
season: Planted at the start of the rains, around May to July. Many plants only start flowering as the days get shorter late in the year, so the main pod season is the cooler months.
material: Seed from fully dry pods. The seed coat is hard, so farmers soak the seed overnight or nick its coat before planting.
spacing: Hills about a meter apart along a pole row, a frame or a fence, with one or two plants a hill.
water: Rainfed in the wet season, with hand watering in long dry spells.
fertilizer: Dried manure or compost at planting and a side dressing of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) or more manure after about a month.
care: Poles or a frame set up early, weeding around the hills, and guiding the vines. Little else.
harvest: Young pods are picked green and tender every few days once bearing starts. Some growers also dig the thick roots of older plants to eat.

ways.label: Direct seeded on poles

steps.title: Dig and add manure
steps.how: Dig the plot or the spots along the fence and mix in dried manure or compost.

steps.title: Soak the seed
steps.how: Soak the seed in water overnight so the hard coat softens.

steps.title: Plant the seed
steps.how: Plant 2 to 3 seeds a hill, with hills about a meter apart, and cover them with 2 to 3 cm of soil.

steps.title: Thin and put up poles
steps.how: Leave the strongest one or two plants and set up bamboo poles about two meters tall or an overhead frame (balag) for the vines.

steps.title: Weed
steps.how: Hoe out the weeds around the hills and pull soil up to the base.

steps.title: Feed
steps.how: Side dress complete fertilizer (14 14 14) or more manure around the plants.

steps.title: Watch for pests
steps.how: Check the flowers and young pods for pod borers and the leaves for leaf spots.

steps.title: Pick the young pods
steps.how: Pick the pods while still tender and green, about two to three weeks after flowering, every few days.

steps.title: Keep seed pods
steps.how: Leave some pods on the vine until they turn brown and dry, then pick and keep the seed.

parts.title: Leave pods on the best vines
parts.how: Stop picking a few well shaped pods on the strongest, healthiest vines and let them hang until they turn brown and dry.

parts.title: Pick before they burst
parts.how: Check the drying pods every few days and pick them once they are brown and papery, before they split open on the vine.

parts.title: Dry and shell
parts.how: Spread the pods on a mat in the sun until brittle, then break them open and take out the hard round seeds.

parts.title: Dry the seed and store it
parts.how: Sun dry the seed once more until it is hard, then keep it in a sealed jar or can in a cool, dry place until the next planting.

ways.note: Day 70 is about the first picking. Plants sown early in the year may wait for shorter days before they flower.

mistakes: Planting the hard seed without soaking, so it comes up slowly and unevenly.
Giving the vines no support, so they tangle on the ground.
Letting pods get old and stringy before picking.
better: Soak or nick the seed and plant into moist, fed soil.
Set up strong poles or a frame before the vines run.
Pick young pods often to keep the plant bearing.
Plant at the start of the rains so the vines are big when the flowering season comes.

watering.traditional: Sigarilyas is mostly a backyard and fence crop planted with the rains and watered by hand only in long dry spells. Once the vines are big, most families leave it to the rain.
watering.method: Hand watering with a can or a hose at the base of each hill, in the early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant at the start of the rains, from May to July, so the vine grows in the wet months and bears in the cooler months that follow. Mulch around the hills to hold the moisture.
watering.dryseason: Vines bearing into the dry months need a watering every few days. Water when the leaves droop in the morning or the soil is dry a finger deep.
watering.wet: Plant on mounds or raised spots so rain drains away, since standing water rots the roots and the tubers. Wet weather also spreads leaf spots, so keep the vines thinned and airy.

schedule.often: Water at planting if the soil is dry, then every day or two until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the hill moist, never soggy
schedule.why: The soaked seed needs steady moisture to come up.

schedule.often: Usually the rains are enough. In a dry spell, water when the topsoil dries
schedule.amount: A watering can of about 10 liters shared among a few hills
schedule.why: Steady growth builds a big vine that bears longer.

schedule.often: In dry weeks, water every few days
schedule.amount: Soak the soil around each hill
schedule.why: Dry soil drops the flowers and gives tough, fibrous pods.

critical: Coming up, the first two weeks: keep the hill moist.
Flowering and podding: dry soil drops flowers and makes the pods tough.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and curl, flowers drop and pods come out short and stringy.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, rotting roots and a vine that stops growing.

better: Mulch the hills with dry grass or rice straw so each watering lasts longer.
Water steadily through flowering and podding instead of only when the vine wilts.
